research_experience.title: Graduate Research — Activation Steering for Automatic Program Repair
research_experience.description: Applied and implemented a training-free activation steering technique (representation engineering, from published research) in PyTorch to improve CodeLLM reliability for bug-fixing. Hands-on work was tuning the steering strength per model across 40+ layer-and-strength configurations on an HPC Slurm cluster, and evaluating on HumanEval and Defects4J across CodeLlama and Qwen. No model weights were retrained.
research_experience.plain_summary: I took an existing method called activation steering — nudging a model's internal signals as it generates, without retraining it — and applied it to two open-source coding models, CodeLlama and Qwen. My hands-on work was dialing in the steering strength for each model and testing it against a standard coding benchmark (HumanEval) and a set of real-world software bugs (Defects4J) until the models produced more correct, reliably compiling code. It raised first-try success by about 8 points on CodeLlama and cut invalid, non-compiling output to near zero, holding across both model families.
research_experience.contribution_scope: Applied and tuned a published technique; the method itself (activation steering / representation engineering) is prior work, not my own invention.
research_experience.novel_finding: Middle transformer layers optimal for code generation tasks; late layers optimal for repair tasks — suggesting task-dependent reasoning stages in CodeLLM architecture.

projects.name: Resume Desk: AI Resume Tailoring Agent
projects.source: Personal project, built for his own job search (the Resume Crafting folder)
projects.status: Local desktop app in daily use; not on GitHub
projects.description: A local app that turns a job post into a tailored, one-page resume. Python checks the post first (work authorization, duplicates, skills matched and missing), then a LangGraph agent picks bullets from a bank of pre-written, fact-checked sentences, and the app stops twice for his approval before it builds the PDF. Every LLM output passes deterministic checks for invented facts, AI-sounding wording, and company-internal jargon. Every resume is logged to his Obsidian job tracker, a side panel answers application-form questions from the chosen resume, and a slide-out panel traces the tokens, cost, and latency of every model call.
projects.contribution_scope: He designed the workflow, the rules, and the checks, and reviewed and tested every change. Much of the code was written with Claude Code as an AI pair programmer, which is how he normally works.

components.triage: Rule-based Python read of a job post: flags citizenship or clearance requirements, no-sponsorship language, and contract or 1099 roles; checks the tracker for duplicates; matches skills against an 82-entry skill dictionary; reads pay, years asked, and role family.
components.bullet_bank: 41 pre-written, humanized resume bullets plus summaries and skill sets, grouped by role family (AI Builder, AI Engineer, Software / Full-stack). New text from each build is saved automatically, with an 80% similarity filter against duplicates and a backup before every save.
components.evidence_check: Grades each keyword from the job post as proven by a bullet, only listed in skills, missing, or a gap he doesn't have, and writes an HTML evidence map with the proving phrase underlined.
components.pdf_builder: Fills an HTML template and prints it with headless Edge, trying spacing levels until the resume fills exactly one page, after a style check for em-dashes, buzzwords, and repeated opening verbs.
components.agent: LangGraph graph with two human-in-the-loop pauses (go or skip after the fit read; vote, edit, or swap bullets before the build), Pydantic structured outputs, up to three validated retries with a fallback to the engine's own picks, and a trim loop when the page runs long.
components.grounding_check: Rejects LLM-written text that contains a number not found in his profile or names a skill he doesn't have.
components.feedback_loop: Votes, edits, swaps, and interview outcomes re-rank bullets for each role family, and recent edits are fed to the model as style examples. Feedback is exported as prompt / chosen / rejected pairs for possible future preference training (no model training yet).
components.model_switching: Each step can run on a different model from Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), or OpenAI (GPT) through LangChain, set in one config file or per run, with per-step reasoning effort, an automatic retry that drops a setting a model rejects (temperature or effort), and an offline fake model for tests.
components.desktop_app: FastAPI backend with a plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript front end, opened in its own window with pywebview from a desktop shortcut. Includes a resizable side panel that answers application questions using his Application Form Filler skill, the chosen resume, and that job's post.
components.humanizer_engine: Deterministic Python cleaner built from his humanizer skill: turns em and en dashes, curly quotes, arrows, and markdown into plain punctuation, and flags AI wording (buzzwords, not-X-but-Y contrasts, tacked-on -ing phrases, chatbot phrases). Flagged text gets one targeted LLM retry, and the build refuses a resume that still fails. Also used to clean the whole bullet bank.
components.jargon_check: Flags company-internal product names from his current job (for example the assistant's internal name) so every bullet describes what a feature does for users in words a recruiter outside the company understands.
components.rephrase_engine: One-click LLM rephrase during review, fenced by checks: the rewrite must keep every keyword the line proved (same patterns as the evidence check), keep every number, pass the grounding check and the humanizer rules, and fit two lines, or the original stays.
components.voice_profile: His resume voice, distilled from his 10 most recent hand-tuned resumes (action verb, then a 'so' outcome, real engineering detail, exact numbers), is injected into every prompt that writes resume text.
components.usage_tracing: Logs every real model call's input, cached, output, and thinking tokens, latency, and cost from a per-model price table, against a monthly budget, prepaid credits, and OpenAI's daily free-token tier. Shown in a slide-out panel with per-step and per-model breakdowns and a toast for each new call.
components.langsmith_tracing: LangSmith tracing turns on when a key is present: one trace per job, grouped by thread, with every LLM call named and tagged by step and model. Prompts, answers, and run errors are scrubbed before upload; testing against a local stand-in server found that LangGraph's pause records carried the whole review screen, which is now reduced to the exception type.
components.prompt_caching: The application-question panel sends its fixed context (skill rules, resume, profile facts, job post) as a cached prefix; a live test read 8,403 of 8,453 input tokens from cache on the second question.

engineering_notes: Every LLM step is followed by a Python check, so the model never has the last word on what goes on the resume
Found and fixed a retry bug where the agent re-checked a failed attempt's output instead of the clean starter order
Found that test runs were leaking invented text into the real bullet bank; offline test runs now never write to it
Fixed a desktop window that opened taller than a 125%-scaled laptop screen by sizing it to the screen
Fixed a Windows console crash on emoji from the tracker by forcing UTF-8 output
Fixed a crash where newer Claude models rejected the temperature setting, by skipping it for those models and retrying without any setting a provider rejects
Found that LangGraph pause events leaked resume text into LangSmith through the error field, and added a scrubber that sends only the exception type
Capped the CLI's final trace upload at 10 seconds after a broken tracing endpoint made it hang on exit
Caught two plain-language rewrites that silently dropped keyword evidence (LLM, AI agent, real-time) by diffing matched keywords before and after
highlights: LangGraph agent that tailors a resume to a job post and stops twice for human approval before anything is built
Python checks after every LLM step: valid bullet ids, house style rules, and a grounding check against invented numbers or skills
Keyword-to-evidence check that shows which bullet proves each skill the job post asks for
Bullet bank that learns from every build, with duplicate detection and suggestions by role family
Human feedback loop: votes, edits, swaps, and interview outcomes re-rank bullets; data saved in DPO format
Packaged as a local desktop app with a resizable side panel that answers application-form questions
Per-step model switching across Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI, with reasoning effort per step and an offline fake model for testing
Humanizer engine and internal-jargon check that keep every bullet and form answer in plain, recruiter-readable language
Guarded LLM rephrase that must keep every keyword, number, and fact the original line had
Token, cost, and latency tracing for every model call, in a slide-out panel and in LangSmith with private data scrubbed

phases.phase_1_setup: Installed Hermes Agent v0.18.2 on Windows, connected the nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b free model through OpenRouter, and ran the terminal TUI. phases.phase_2_mobile: Launched Hermes WebUI via bootstrap.py with HERMES_WEBUI_HOST set to 0.0.0.0 so the server accepted LAN connections. Found that raw API access alone produced generic responses with no structure. Authored a custom SKILL.md that gave the agent procedural formatting rules: pull GitHub commits and calendar events, filter noise, and compile a structured Markdown weekly review. Scheduled it to run autonomously every Friday at 5 PM UTC (cron: 0 17 * * 5), delivering results directly to the Hermex mobile app.

research_paper.title: Automatic Program Repair Through Activation Steering
research_paper.subtitle: A Research Project on Enhancing Code Generation through Neural Network Steering
research_paper.abstract_summary: Training-free method for improving CodeLLM reliability using Activation Steering (Representation Engineering). Computes a correctness vector from contrastive buggy/correct code pairs and injects it into residual streams via PyTorch forward hooks at inference time.

benchmarks.Defects4J: 565 real-world Java bugs (pass@1 against full test suite)

novel_findings: Code correctness is a steerable, linearly-represented concept in CodeLLM activation space
Middle layers optimal for generation tasks (HumanEval); late layers optimal for repair tasks (Defects4J)
Activation steering eliminates invalid/non-compiling output without any model retraining
limitations: Requires white-box model access (not usable with GPT-4 API)
Hyperparameter grid search needed per new model

target_company_types: Austin-based tech with active AI division

career_narrative.identity: Software and AI engineer who ships AI features in real products, along with the clean data going in and the human review step coming out.

story_arc.what: Python and SQL pipelines, Pandas/NumPy preprocessing, and validation checks that analytics and ML work ran on.
Now Assist incident summaries and knowledge drafts, Flow Designer automation, Vertex AI through the Generative AI Controller, and Python checks against source records.
Activation steering in PyTorch: CodeLlama-7B HumanEval 48.12% to 56.25% and invalid output 4.38% to zero, without retraining.
React and TypeScript front end and the Python AI service behind ticket and user story generation, with a review step before anything is saved.

career_narrative.thirty_second_pitch: I'm a software and AI engineer with about three years of experience shipping AI features in real products. I'm a founding engineer at VelocitiPM, where I build the React and TypeScript front end and the Python service behind its AI ticket generation. Before that I rolled out generative AI incident summarization at ServiceNow as a co-op, and at Cognizant I built the Python and SQL pipelines that analytics and machine learning work ran on. In my master's research at Iowa State I used activation steering to raise CodeLlama-7B's HumanEval accuracy by 8 points without retraining. In every one of those jobs, the AI part only worked as well as the data going into it and the review step after it, so that's what I build for.

Works across the stack: React and TypeScript front end, Python AI services, Supabase and PostgreSQL
